questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Explain Four (4) ways by which trade between countries is restricted:

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Trade restrictions (protectionism) are measures used by a government to limit imports, and sometimes exports, in order to protect domestic producers or the balance of payments. The main ways are the following.

1. **Tariffs (customs duties).** A tax placed on imported goods when they enter the country. It raises the price of the imported good, so that consumers buy less of it and more of the home-produced good. Example: a customs duty on imported rice or second-hand clothes.

2. **Quotas.** A **physical limit** on the quantity or value of a good that may be imported (or exported) in a given period. Once the quota is filled, no more can enter, whatever the price. Example: a limit on the tonnes of imported sugar allowed in one year.

3. **Embargo or prohibition.** A **total ban** on trade in a particular good or with a particular country, for reasons of security, health, morals or politics. Example: a ban on imports of harmful drugs or of weapons, or a ban on trade with a country under sanctions.

4. **Exchange control.** The government limits the amount of foreign currency that importers may buy, or requires a licence to obtain it, so that only approved imports can be paid for.

5. **Import licensing and administrative barriers.** Importers must obtain a licence or pass slow customs procedures, health and quality inspections and complicated documentation, which discourages imports.

6. **Subsidies to domestic producers.** Payments by the government to local producers lower their costs and prices, so that imported goods cannot compete with them. Example: subsidised fertiliser for local farmers.

(The candidate needs only four of these ways, each explained.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Explain any Three (3) reasons why a country will impose restrictions on international trade,

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A country restricts trade for the following reasons.

1. **To protect infant industries.** New domestic industries have high costs because they are small and inexperienced. Restrictions give them time to grow, gain economies of scale and become able to compete with foreign firms.

2. **To prevent dumping.** Foreign firms may sell goods abroad at prices below their cost, or below the price in their home market, in order to drive local firms out of business. Duties or quotas protect local producers from this unfair competition.

3. **To protect employment.** Limiting imports increases the demand for locally produced goods and so protects existing jobs and creates new ones in domestic industries.

4. **To correct a balance of payments deficit.** Restricting imports reduces the money leaving the country and so reduces the deficit on the current account.

5. **To raise government revenue.** Customs duties on imports are an important and easily collected source of income for the government, especially in developing countries.

6. **For national security, health and self-sufficiency.** Strategic industries (food, defence) are protected so that the country does not depend on foreign supplies, and harmful or unsafe goods are kept out.

(Any three, each explained.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(ii) Advance any Three (3) reasons why trade restrictions should be eliminated

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Free trade has the following advantages, which are the reasons for removing restrictions.

1. **Wider choice and lower prices for consumers.** Without duties and quotas, imported goods are cheaper and more varied, so the real income and standard of living of consumers rise.

2. **Specialisation and comparative advantage.** Each country can specialise in what it produces at the lowest opportunity cost and trade for the rest, so that world output and income are higher than under restrictions.

3. **Greater efficiency through competition.** Protected industries have no pressure to cut costs or improve quality; foreign competition forces firms to become more efficient and to innovate.

4. **Larger markets and economies of scale.** Producers can sell to the world market, produce on a larger scale and lower their average cost.

5. **Avoidance of retaliation.** Restrictions may provoke other countries to restrict our exports in return, so that everyone loses (a trade war).

6. **Less smuggling and corruption, and access to raw materials and technology.** High barriers encourage smuggling and bribery, and restrict the inputs and machines that local firms need.

(Any three, each advanced with a reason.)
